presentation_slides.unit_title: Development of Capitalism and Nationalism from 1815 to 1914

slides.title: UNIT ONE: Development of Capitalism and Nationalism from 1815 to 1914
content: In this unit, you will learn about:
• The nature and main characteristic features of capitalism
• Factors that led to the Industrial Revolution and its political and socio-economic results
• Factors contributing to the growth of nationalism in the nineteenth century
• The unification of Italy and Germany as major manifestations of nationalism
• Imperialism as one of the main features of the second half of the nineteenth century
• The causes, course, and consequences of the American Civil War
• The nature of the 'Eastern Question' and the Balkan Wars

slides.title: Development of Capitalism: Nature and Main Features
content: Capitalism grew in the womb of decaying feudalism and became the dominant economic system in the Western world since the breakup of feudalism.
• Fully fledged capitalism emerged in Northwestern Europe, especially in Great Britain and the Netherlands, from the 16th to 17th centuries
• Mercantilism was established during this period (distribution of goods bought at a certain price and sold at a higher price to generate profits)
• The Protestant Reformation of the 16th century helped consolidate capitalism
• The rise of strong nation-states supported capitalism through regulations, uniform monetary systems, and public investment

slides.title: Main Features of Capitalism
content: 1. Private ownership of the means of production, especially in the industrial sector
2. Split between two antagonistic classes:
• Capitalist class (owners of property, plants, and equipment)
• Working class (sold their labor for wages)
3. Use of accumulated capital to enlarge productive capacity rather than unproductive enterprises
4. Profit motive - companies make goods and services only for profits
5. Laissez-faire - belief that markets should operate without government intervention

slides.title: Classical Capitalism vs. Marxian Economics
content: Adam Smith (1723-1790):
• Scottish economist and moral philosopher considered a forefather of capitalism
• Wrote 'An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations' (1776)
• Recommended leaving economic decisions to free play of self-regulating market forces
Karl Marx (Marxian Economics):
• Believed capitalism brings about class segregation between capitalist and working class
• Exploitation of surplus value of labor is a major drawback
• Predicted capitalism would weaken in systematic crises
• Predicted the inevitable overthrow of capitalism in a proletarian-led class war

slides.title: The Industrial Revolution: Origins and Development
content: The Industrial Revolution was the first establishment of industrial capitalism in any country.
• Took place in Britain between 1750/1780 and 1850
• Preceded by changes going back to the mid-16th century and even to the Middle Ages
• By 1850, Britain was already a mature industrial state
Key Changes:
• Organizational: Shift from putting-out system to new factory system
• Technological: Introduction of machinery and steam power
• Result: Far greater and cheaper mass production

slides.title: The Factory System and Technology
content: Factory System:
• Production concentrated in large units (factories)
• Industrial capitalist owned the factory, built machinery, processed raw materials
• Workers owned only their labor power, sold for money wages
• More productive and profitable than earlier systems
Technology:
• Inanimate power from water and wind
• Steam power (Newcomen's engine 1705/1709, James Watt's engine 1783/84)
• Railways - first modern railway (Liverpool and Manchester, opened 1830)
• By 1850, a network of railways connected all important places in Britain

slides.title: Political and Socio-Economic Consequences
content: Economic:
• Overproduction became the main economic problem
• Agriculture less dominant in advanced countries
• Agricultural productivity increased through better methods and science
Social:
• Rapid urbanization - shift from countryside to towns and cities
• Rapid population expansion
• New class system with greater class consciousness:
- Industrial capitalist class (added to bourgeoisie)
- Industrial proletariat (wage workers in factories)

slides.title: Global Impacts of the Industrial Revolution
content: Political and International:
• Growth of socialism and working class political parties
• Industry, technology, and science applied to armies and navies
• Gap in power between Western and non-Western states grew bigger
• Western states became more interested in non-Western areas as sources of raw materials and markets
Imperialism:
• Improved transport and communications (steamships, railways, electric telegraph)
• The world became one single integrated capitalist world economy
• Led to the New Imperialism of the late 19th century - expanding drive for colonial acquisitions

slides.title: Nationalism: Growth and Features
content: Nationalism has been the most powerful political force since the 1850s.
• Deepest roots lie in a shared sense of regional and cultural identity expressed in custom, language, and religion
• Influenced all classes but more so the urban than rural peasants
Factors promoting growth:
• Compulsory primary education used for state building and inculcating patriotism
• Compulsory military service
• Cheap newspapers for the masses (often chauvinistic)
• Literature (strongly nationalist)
• Patriotic societies
• Wars of unification (Italy, Germany) and national liberation (Balkans)

slides.title: Social Darwinism and Transformation of Nationalism (1880s-1914)
content: Social Darwinism:
• Pseudo-science that stimulated nationalism
• History is a struggle between states and nations for power, supremacy, and survival
• Strongest states would be victors; weak states would be subjugated
Transformation of Nationalism (1880s-1914):
• More national movements appeared, tending towards fragmentation rather than unity
• Language and ethnicity became major criteria
• National question became part of domestic politics of many states (especially multi-nationals)
• Nationalism was a two-edged weapon: strengthened loyalty but also caused discontent among minorities

slides.title: Unification of Italy: Background and Obstacles
content: Background:
• Began with the Congress of Vienna (1815), ended with the Franco-Prussian War (1871)
• In 1852, Italy was still politically divided
• Austrian influence was supreme in the north
Obstacles to Unification:
• Power of Austria (wanted to maintain the status quo)
• Weakness of national sentiment in Italy
Favorable Factors:
• Diplomatic isolation of Austria after the Crimean War (1855-56)
• Rivalries between France and Austria in Italy

slides.title: Key Figures: Cavour and Garibaldi
content: Camillo Cavour (1810-61):
• Prime Minister of Piedmont (1852-62)
• Main architect of Italian unification 'from above'
• Prepared Piedmont for leadership role
• 1858: Reached an agreement (Plombieres) with Napoleon III for an alliance against Austria
• April 1859: Provoked Austria to declare war on Piedmont
• Successfully gained control of Lombardy, Tuscany, Parma, and Modena
Giuseppe Garibaldi:
• Successful military leader
• Led the Thousand Volunteers
• Invaded Sicily (1860) and captured Naples (September 7, 1860)

slides.title: Garibaldi's Success and Completion of Unification
content: Reasons for Garibaldi's Success:
• Skill as a leader in guerrilla warfare and magnetic personality
• Successful mobilization of the Sicilian masses
• Demoralization of the army of Naples and defeatism of officials
Completion of Unification:
• February 18, 1861: Victor Emmanuel assumed the title of King of Italy
• 1866: Used the Austro-Prussian War to gain Venetia (Italy allied with Prussia)
• 1870-71: Used the Franco-Prussian War to seize Rome (French troops withdrew)
• Rome became the capital of Italy

slides.title: Unification of Germany: Background and Obstacles
content: Background:
• In the 1850s, Germany was a loose confederation of 39 states (the German Confederation/Bund)
• The Bund was presided over by Austria, with Prussia second
• German nationalists wanted real political unity for nationalist and economic reasons
Obstacles to Unification:
• Austria wanted to preserve the status quo
• German princes wanted to keep their independence
• Cultural differences between North and South Germany

slides.title: Otto von Bismarck and His Strategies
content: Otto von Bismarck (1815-1898):
• Appointed chief minister of Prussia by King William I
• Politically conservative but a political realist and extremely able
• Overcame the constitutional crisis by collecting taxes without Parliament's consent
Bismarck's Strategies:
• Knew Germany could not be united without war against Austria and France
• Maintained good relations with Russia (common interest in opposing Polish nationalism)
• Used three military successes to unite Germany:
1. War with Denmark (1864) - acquired Schleswig-Holstein
2. Austro-Prussian War (1866) - excluded Austria, formed North German Confederation
3. Franco-Prussian War (1870-71) - proclamation of German Empire (1871)

slides.title: The American Civil War: Origins and Divisive Issues
content: Background:
• Fought from 1861 to 1865
• Between the 23 Northern states (Union) and 11 Southern states (Confederacy)
Divisive Issues:
• Economic dominance of the North
• Tariffs: South wanted low tariffs; North wanted protective tariffs
• States' rights vs. National Federal Government
• The slavery issue outweighed all others (capable of producing secession and civil war)
Trigger:
• 1860: Abraham Lincoln elected President
• South saw this as an intolerable threat to slavery
• Seven states seceded before Lincoln took office

slides.title: The Civil War and Its Results
content: Union Advantages:
• More states, bigger population, more skilled labor
• Far more industry and railways
• Much greater agricultural production (except cotton)
• Naval power to block the South
• European governments did not intervene
Key Events:
• Emancipation Proclamation (January 1, 1863): All slaves in rebel-held territory would be free
• Helped the North recruit African American troops
• April 1865: Confederacy defeated unconditionally
• April 14, 1865: Lincoln assassinated by John Wilkes Booth

slides.title: Constitutional Amendments and Legacy
content: Results of the Civil War:
• Ended secession and slavery once and for all
Constitutional Amendments:
• Thirteenth Amendment: Abolished slavery
• Fourteenth Amendment: Granted citizenship to former slaves
• Fifteenth Amendment: Allowed former slaves to vote
Significance:
• Southern political leaders had virtually no impact on post-war decisions
• Strengthened the power of the National Federal Government

slides.title: The Eastern Question: Definition and Background
content: The 'Eastern Question' meant what would happen to the Ottoman Empire in the Balkans and elsewhere as Ottoman power declined.
Key Features:
• Ottoman Empire was threatened by Balkan national movements, usually backed by Russia
• An issue of political and economic instability from the late 18th to early 20th centuries
• Main cause of strategic competition among European great powers
European Interests:
• Russia: Wanted to benefit from Ottoman collapse
• Austria-Hungary and Britain: Wanted the Empire's preservation as in their best interests

slides.title: The Eastern Question: Major Events and Treaties
content: 1870s: Ottoman hardships increased (empty treasury, insurrections in Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Serbia, Montenegro)
Treaty of San Stefano (March 3, 1878):
• Stipulated independence for Romania, Serbia, and Montenegro
• Autonomy for Bulgaria
• Reforms in Bosnia and Herzegovina
• Large indemnity to Russia
• Would give Russia great influence in Southeastern Europe
Treaty of Berlin (July 13, 1878):
• Boundaries adjusted in Ottoman Empire's favor
• Bulgaria divided into two states (to prevent Russian domination)
• Bosnia and Herzegovina transferred to Austrian control
• Germany drew away from Russia and became closer to Austria-Hungary (Dual Alliance, 1879)

slides.title: The Balkan Wars (1912-1913)
content: First Balkan War (October 8, 1912 - May 30, 1913):
• Serbia, Montenegro, Bulgaria, and Greece formed the Balkan League with Russian support
• Attacked the Ottoman Empire to take Macedonia
• Allies were soon victorious
• Treaty of London (May 30, 1913): Ottoman Empire lost almost all remaining European territory
Second Balkan War (June 29-July 30, 1913):
• Bulgaria vs. Serbia and Greece (later joined by Romania and the Ottoman Empire)
• Over partitioning of Macedonia
• Treaty of Bucharest (August 10, 1913): Greece and Serbia divided most of Macedonia
Consequences:
• Greece gained southern Macedonia and Crete
• Serbia gained Kosovo and extended into Macedonia
• Albania was made an independent state
• Marked by ethnic cleansing and atrocities

slides.title: UNIT TWO: Africa and the Colonial Experience (1880s - 1960s)
content: This unit discusses the main historical developments in Africa from the 1880s to the 1960s.
Key Lessons:
• The Era of 'Legitimate Trade' and Colonial Empires
• African Resistance against Colonial Expansion
• Colonial Administration and the Colonial States
Key Concepts:
• Colonialism, Process of Colonization, Resistance
• Legitimate Trade, Direct Rule, Indirect Rule

slides.section: 2.1 The Era of 'Legitimate Trade' and Colonial Empires
slides.title: The Birth and Expansion of the 'Legitimate Trade'
content: The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade was referred to as the 'Illegitimate Trade'.
After the end of the slave trade:
• Europeans introduced a new trade called the 'Legitimate Trade'
• Principal commodities: gum, groundnuts, palm (palm oil became West Africa's major export)
Impact of 'Legitimate Trade':
• Did not economically prosper West African states
• Benefited most African rulers and wealthy merchants
• Did not bring significant improvement to the majority of West Africans
• Imported European goods (cloth, alcoholic drinks, firearms) weakened indigenous industries
• European merchants controlled both export and internal trade

slides.section: 2.1 The Era of 'Legitimate Trade' and Colonial Empires
slides.title: The Infrastructure and Ideology of New Imperialism
content: New Imperialism: A period of increased expansion of capitalism from the second half of the 19th century to WWI.
Factors Driving New Imperialism:
• Economic: Financial crisis of the early 1870s
• Political: European states wanted to protect economic interests
• Technological: More advanced technology (firearms, communication, medicine)
• Industrial: Need for raw materials and markets for manufactured goods
European Presence in Africa Before the 1870s:
• Contacts were limited to coastal areas
• Europeans lacked efficient firearms and means to control the interior
• Tsetse fly and mosquito prevented penetration

slides.section: 2.1 The Era of 'Legitimate Trade' and Colonial Empires
slides.title: Technological Advances and European Expansion
content: Technological Advances that Enabled European Penetration:
• Better river boats and steamships
• Better rifles and firearms
• Discovery of medicine to combat malaria
Impact:
• By 1880, a small number of well-armed European soldiers could defeat native Africans with numerical superiority
• Industrial development invited new powers (Germany, Italy) to the colonial contest
Great Britain's Position:
• First country to embark on the industrial revolution
• Strongest world power with supremacy in military and naval powers
• Built more efficient naval force (other powers followed)

slides.section: 2.1 The Era of 'Legitimate Trade' and Colonial Empires
slides.title: The Partition of Africa: Motives and Processes
content: Motives for the Scramble for Africa:
• Economic: Markets for products, suppliers of natural resources
• Political: National pride and balance of power
• Technological: Advances in firearms, transportation, communication
• Medical: Advances in medicine enabled longer stays in the tropics
Berlin Conference (1884-1885):
• Initiated by Bismarck of Germany
• Involved 13 European countries (no African country invited)
• Goals: Settle Congo claims, resolve Anglo-French rivalries along the Niger River
• Established rules for acquiring African territory
• Article 36: Obligated colonial powers to notify each other when claiming African territory

slides.section: 2.1 The Era of 'Legitimate Trade' and Colonial Empires
slides.title: Results of the Berlin Conference
content: Key Outcomes (February 25, 1885):
• King Leopold II of Belgium secured ownership of the Congo Free State
• France got acceptance of its claims to the French-Congo
• Portugal lost most of its Congo claims
• Germany's new protectorates recognized (Togoland, Cameroon, Southwest Africa)
General Act of Berlin:
• Declared free trade along the Congo Basin
• Free navigation on the Niger River
• 'Effective occupation' necessary for claims to remain valid
Significance:
• Formalized the partition of Africa
• Laid the groundwork for the physical occupation of territories

slides.title: African Initiatives and Responses to Colonialism
content: Africans did not welcome the European colonizers.
Methods of Colonization Used by Europeans:
• Fake treaties
• Use of force when treaties failed
African Reactions:
• Peaceful methods
• Violent methods
• Resistance in almost every region of European advance
Ideological Basis of Resistance:
• Attempt to safeguard their sovereignty
The only successful anti-colonial struggle in Africa was that of Ethiopia (Battle of Adwa, 1896)

slides.title: Samori Toure of Mandinka
content: Samori Toure (c. 1828 - June 2, 1900):
• Muslim religious figure and military leader
• Founder of the Wassoulou Empire (present-day Guinea, Sierra Leone, Cote d'Ivoire, Burkina Faso)
• Strongly resisted French colonial rule in West Africa
Military Strategy:
• Imported firearms via Freetown (Sierra Leone) since 1876
• Controlled the Bure gold mine district (increased economic strength)
• Organized well-trained army with infantry and cavalry
Key Events:
• 1882: Repulsed French attack
• 1885: Sought British protection (refused) but got weapons
• 1891-1898: Fought French, eventually lost the empire
• September 29, 1898: Surrendered to the French
• Died in captivity in Gabon (June 2, 1900)

slides.title: The Ashanti
content: The Ashanti Empire (present-day Ghana):
• Emerged in the 17th century
• Osei Tutu (Asantehene, 1701-1717) unified independent chiefdoms
• Golden Stool: Symbolized the ancestors of all Ashanti
Economy:
• Gold was the major product (gold dust became the currency)
• By the early 1800s, became a major exporter of enslaved people
Resistance and Defeat:
• From 1790 until 1896, continuously at war
• 1823-1873: Resisted British advance
• 1874: British captured Kumasi briefly
• 1897: Conquered again
• 1900: Final uprising, annexed into Gold Coast colony (1902)

slides.title: Urabi Pasha's Rebellion in Egypt
content: Ahmed Urabi (Urabi Pasha):
• An officer in the Egyptian army
• Led the Urabi revolt (1879-1882) against the Anglo-French dual rule
Objectives:
• Social justice for Egyptians
• Free Egypt and Sudan from foreign control
• End the absolutist regime of the Khedive
Outcome:
• 1882: British bombardment and occupation of Egypt
• Urabi captured and exiled to Ceylon (Sri Lanka)
• Returned to Egypt in 1901, died in 1911
Significance:
• First instance of nationalistic sentiments in Egypt
• Laid the foundation for mass politics in Egypt
• Urabi regarded as an Egyptian patriot and national hero

slides.title: The Mahadist Movement in Sudan
content: Muhammad Ahmad (Al-Mahdi):
• Muslim holy man from Dongola
• Declared himself the expected Mahdi (Islamic savior)
Key Events:
• August 12, 1881: Victory at the Battle of Aba
• November 1883: Victory over Anglo-Egyptian army in Kordofan
• 1885: Captured Khartoum and killed Charles Gordon
• Five months later, Muhammad Ahmad died
After Al-Mahdi's Death:
• Khalifa Abdullah took leadership
• Set up a strong administrative system based on Quranic rules
Final Defeat:
• 1896-1898: Anglo-Egyptian army under General Kitchener
• 1898: Defeated Mahadists at the Battle of Omdurman
• Sudan occupied by combined British and Egyptian forces
• Anglo-Egyptian Condominium established

slides.title: The Maji-Maji Rebellion
content: Maji-Maji Rebellion (1905-1907):
• Occurred in Tanganyika (German East Africa)
• Most serious challenge for the Germans
Causes:
• Imposition of heavy taxes
• Use of forced labor in cotton farms for export
Key Features:
• Spontaneous revolt with no previous planning or central leadership
• Unity of Southern Tanzania peoples (unique in African resistance history)
• Used magic water (Maji-Maji) believed to turn enemy bullets into water
German Response:
• Brought reinforcements from Somaliland and New Guinea
• Pursued 'scorched-earth' policy
• Defeated Ngoni warriors in 1907
Significance:
• Demonstrated possibility of broader African anti-colonial nationalism
• Inspired later generation of nationalists in the 1960s

slides.section: 2.3 Colonial Administration and the Colonial States
slides.title: British Colonial Policy: Indirect Rule
content: Indirect Rule:
• Most clearly formulated by Frederick Lugard
• Described in his book 'The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa' (1922)
Principles:
• Cheapest and most effective way to administer vast territories with minimum European personnel
• Used traditional chiefs (ensured they were traditional rulers)
• Emphasized differences in dialects, rigid 'tribal' distinctions
• Divided, ruled, and reinforced ethnic differences
Impact:
• Made it more difficult for Africans to achieve unity in opposition

slides.section: 2.3 Colonial Administration and the Colonial States
slides.title: French Colonial Policy: Direct Rule
content: Direct Rule/Assimilation Policy:
• Aimed to assimilate colonial peoples into French culture
• In full only in Senegal
Albert Sarraut (Minister of Colonies, 1920-24, 1932-33):
• Laid foundations for 'Direct Rule'
• Less respectful of African personalities but more fraternal
• France and her African colonies must be kept united
Key Differences from British Method:
• French were not keen on using traditional rulers
• French gave less powers to chiefs
• French education was largely state-run (not mission schools)
• All teaching was in French
Result:
• Both methods caused chiefs to lose traditional character and become dependent on colonial masters

slides.section: 2.3 Colonial Administration and the Colonial States
slides.title: Other Colonial Powers in Africa
content: Belgian Colonial Rule:
• Colonial possessions: Congo, Rwanda, Burundi
• Based on 'colonial trinity': state, missionaries, and private companies
Portuguese Colonial Rule:
• Colonies: Angola and Mozambique
• Oppressive and liberal methods
• Assimilation policy never fully implemented
German Colonial Rule:
• Expression of nationalism and moral superiority
• Direct rule (like the French)
• Designed to maximally exploit resources (especially Tanganyika)

slides.section: 2.3 Colonial Administration and the Colonial States
slides.title: The Political Economy of Colonial Agriculture
content: Driving Factors:
• Need for raw materials for European industries
• New markets for manufactured goods
Cash Crops:
• Peasants forced to undertake cash crop production
• Chiefs given task of establishing export plantations (using unpaid labor)
• Major cash crops: palm oil, palm kernels, peanuts, cocoa, coffee, cotton
Impact on Peasants:
• African peasant farmers had to pay more for what they bought
• With failing real incomes, more land had to be brought into cash-crop production
• Food crops neglected, soil became exhausted
• In times of drought, famine struck (e.g., Niger 1931 killed nearly half the population)
Example: Southern Sudan (British Scheme):
• Peasants lost access to food-growing land
• Only received 40% of profits from their cotton

slides.section: 2.3 Colonial Administration and the Colonial States
slides.title: The Political Economy of Colonial Mining and Trade
content: Mining:
• Most profitable sector for capital investment
• Colonial authorities assumed all rights over minerals, then leased to European-owned companies
Major Mining Regions:
• Gold fields of Asante
• Tin-mines of Jos plateau (Nigeria)
• Katanga (Shaba) and Northern Rhodesia (Zambia) 'copper belt'
- Controlled by Union Miniere Company
• Southern Rhodesia: gold, copper, asbestos
• Witwatersrand: dominant industrial mining center of southern Africa
Trade:
• African markets disoriented
• Indigenous market centers weakened or died
• Colonial powers established new marketing centers and trade routes
• Made African trade mainly export-import oriented

presentation_slides.unit_title: Social, Economic and Political Developments in Ethiopia, Mid, 19th C. to 1941

slides.title: UNIT THREE: Social, Economic and Political Developments in Ethiopia, Mid, 19th C. to 1941
content: This unit discusses the main historical developments in Ethiopia and the Horn of Africa from 1855 to 1941.
Key Topics:
• Long-distance trade and people's interaction in the 19th century
• Power rivalry and consolidating central government (1855-1913)
• Shift of political center from the north to Shewa
• Territorial expansion
• External relations, challenges, and threats
• The victory of Adwa
• Religious doctrinal controversies
• Birth of Eritrea as an Italian colony
• Power struggles among ruling elites (1906-1936)
• Italian aggression and patriotic resistance

slides.section: 3.1 Long Distance Trade and Peoples' Interaction
slides.title: Long Distance Trade in 19th Century Ethiopia
content: Factors for Revival:
• Establishment of monarchical system among southwestern Oromo regions (five Oromo kingdoms in the Gibe region)
• Relative improvement of political conditions along the Red Sea coast
• Egyptian conquest of South Arabia at the beginning of the 19th century
Major Caravan Routes:
1. Bonga (Kafa) - Jimma - Saka - Assendabo - Basso - Gondar
• Gondar - Metemma - Sudan
• Gondar - Adwa - Massawa
2. Bonga - Jimma - Saka - Assendabo - Aussa - Tajura/Obock
3. Bonga - Jimma - Soddo - Ankober - Harar - Zeila/Berbera

slides.section: 3.1 Long Distance Trade and Peoples' Interaction
slides.title: Trade Items, Slave Trade, and People's Interaction
content: Major Trading Items:
• Ivory, civet, gold, wax, animal skins, and slaves
• Coffee became important by the last quarter of the 19th century
Slave Trade:
• Slaves were a major Ethiopian export since ancient times
• Exported to both Sudan and Arabia
• Well-known slave auction markets: Yejjube (Gojjam), Abdul Rasul (near Aleyu Amba)
Merchants:
• Majority were Muslim traders from northern Ethiopia (Jabarti)
• Later faced competition from Afkala (dominant Muslim merchants in southwestern Ethiopia)
Trade as a Factor for People's Interaction:
• Introduced Islam to the Gibe region
• Helped Oromo chiefs establish monarchies and legitimize power
• Created strong links between northern and southwestern Ethiopia
• Exchange of ideas and cultures

slides.section: 3.2 Power Rivalry and Consolidating Central Government
slides.title: The Zemene Mesafint (Era of Princes)
content: Zemene Mesafint (1769-1855):
• Period of intense regionalism
• Country divided into several almost independent regional polities
• Power of the Solomonic kings thoroughly weakened
• Yejju Rases (Worashe) dominated Ethiopian politics (1769-1855)
Impact on Peasants:
• Forced to attend battles against their will
• Had to hand over produce to lords
• Pay numerous taxes to numerous lords
• Obliged to feed soldiers through the billeting system
• Could not conduct agricultural activities peacefully
Religious Doctrinal Controversies:
• Dispute between House of Abba Ewostatewos and House of Teklehaimanot (Saturday Sabbath)
• Controversies on the birth of Christ (Soset Ledet vs. Hulet Ledet)

slides.section: 3.2 Power Rivalry and Consolidating Central Government
slides.title: Emperor Tewodros II (1855-1868)
content: Kassa Hailu's Rise:
• Defeated regional lords in four major battles:
- Guramba (November 1852): Defeated Dejach Goshu Zewde
- Gorgora Bichen (April 1853): Defeated vassals of Ras Ali Alula
- Ayshal (June 29, 1853): Defeated Ras Ali Alula
- Deresge (February 1855): Defeated Dejach Wube
• Ascended as Tewodros II, King of Kings of Ethiopia
Reforms Attempted:
• Unify the country and introduce centralized administration
• Create a national army
• Modern military training and military drills
• Introduced military titles (AserAleqa, Hamsa Aleqa, Meto Aleqa, Shaleqa)
• Wanted to manufacture firearms locally

slides.section: 3.2 Power Rivalry and Consolidating Central Government
slides.title: Downfall of Emperor Tewodros II
content: Reasons for Downfall:
• Harsh punitive measures against opposition
• Conflict with the Ethiopian Orthodox Church:
- Attempted to confiscate extra land holdings
- Abune Selama excommunicated him
- Tewodros imprisoned the Abune (died in prison, 1867)
• Serious opposition from regional lords
Conflict with Britain:
• Wrote to Queen Victoria for skilled personnel (no response)
• Detained British consul and European missionaries
• Forced them to manufacture mortars at Gafat
British Military Expedition (1867-1868):
• Led by General Robert Napier
• Battle of Arogee (April 10, 1868): Ethiopian forces routed
• April 13, 1868: Tewodros committed suicide at Meqdela
• British looted treasury and took Prince Alemayehu as captive

slides.section: 3.2 Power Rivalry and Consolidating Central Government
slides.title: Emperor Yohannis IV (1872-1889)
content: After Tewodros:
• Three contenders: Dejzmach Kassa Mircha (Tigray), Wagshum Gobezie Gebre Medhin (Lasta), Menilek Haile Melekot (Shewa)
• Wagshum Gobezie took the throne as Emperor Tekle Giorgis (1871) but was defeated by Kassa Mircha at the Battle of Asem (July 1871)
• 1872: Dejzmach Kassa Mircha declared himself Emperor Yohannis IV
Yohannis IV's Rule:
• Politically liberal and followed administration resembling federalism
• Granted great deal of autonomy to regional and dynastic rulers
• 1878: Forced Menilek to drop his title of king of kings and confirmed him as king of Shewa
• 1881: Designated Ras Adal Tesema as Negus of Gojjam and Kafa
External Threats:
• Fought successful wars against Egyptian invaders
• Stopped Italian expansion from Massawa
• Fought against Mahadist forces
• Died in the Battle of Metemma (1889)

slides.section: 3.2 Power Rivalry and Consolidating Central Government
slides.title: Shift of Political Centre from North to Shewa
content: Despite Yohannis IV designating Ras Mengesha as his heir, it was Negus Menilek of Shewa who inherited the throne.
Main Features of Menilek II's Reign:
1. Large-scale territorial expansion to the south, southwest, and southeast
2. Defending the country against colonial aggression (Battle of Adwa, 1896)
3. Process of modernization begun by Tewodros
Achievements:
• Size of the old Christian kingdom more than doubled
• Ethiopia got her first internationally recognized modern boundaries
• Thanks to the victory at Adwa (1896)

slides.section: 3.3 Territorial Expansion and Incorporation of Kingdoms
slides.title: Menilek's Territorial Expansion
content: Phases of Expansion:
• 1870-1889: Began while Menilek was king of Shewa
• 1889-1896: Further expansion
• 1896-1900: Post-Adwa expansion
Incorporated Areas:
• 1870s: Oromo clans of Shewa, Kistane Gurage (peaceful submission)
• Southern Gurage: Stiff resistance under Hassan Enjamo, subdued in 1888
• 1882: Battle of Embabo - Menilek defeated Negus Tekle Haimanot of Gojjam
• 1882-1884: Five Oromo Kingdoms in Gibe region and Leqa states in Wollega submitted peacefully
• Arsi: Stiff resistance
• 1887: Emirate of Harar subdued at the Battle of Chelenqo

slides.section: 3.3 Territorial Expansion and Incorporation of Kingdoms
slides.title: Later Campaigns and Resistance
content: Wolaita Campaign (1894):
• Probably the bloodiest of all campaigns
• Led by Emperor Menilek personally
• People of Wolaita organized under King Kawo Tona
• Put up determined fight, using indigenous warfare techniques
• Kawo Tona captured and became a prisoner for life
Kafa Campaign:
• Conducted after Adwa victory
• Led by Ras Wolde Giorgis
• Kafa people under Tato Gaki Sherecho resisted
• Tato Gaki Sherecho captured and exiled
Post-Adwa Campaigns:
• Incorporated Beni Shangul, Gambella, Borena, and much of the Ogaden
• Sought to check European colonial advance
• Sheikh Abdurrahman Hojele defected to Menilek, aborting united resistance

slides.section: 3.3 Territorial Expansion and Incorporation of Kingdoms
slides.title: Land Tenure Systems: North vs. South
content: Northern Ethiopia:
• Traditional community system of land ownership (communally owned)
• Rist: Hereditary right to hold and use land
• Gult: Right to collect tax (not hereditary initially, later became hereditary)
Southern Ethiopia:
• Gebbar-Melkegna System: Basic means of surplus appropriation
• Gebbar: Land holding peasant who had to pay tribute (giber)
• Melkegna: Gult owner who represented the government
Qelad System:
• Introduced after Menilek's expansion
• Led to land measurement and privatization
• Increased state revenue through land tax classification
• Reduced peasants from land-owing farmers to insecure tenants

slides.title: External Challenges: Egyptian and Italian Aggression
content: Egyptian Aggression (1875-1876):
• Khedive Ismael Pasha launched war of aggression from three directions
• Battle of Gundet (November 16, 1875): Ethiopian victory (complete Egyptian defeat)
• Battle of Gura (March 7-9, 1876): Ethiopian victory (captured 2,500 soldiers and weapons)
• Egyptians still controlled Massawa and Bogos
Hewett Treaty (1884):
• Signed between Yohannis IV and Admiral William Hewett
• Ethiopia agreed to facilitate safe evacuation of Egyptian troops from Sudan
• British promised to return Bogos and make Massawa a free port
• British failed to keep promises - allowed Italy to occupy Massawa
Dogali Incident (1887):
• Ras Alula destroyed an Italian army of about 500 soldiers
• First serious blow to Italian colonial advance
• Italians demanded apology and territory, which Yohannis rejected

slides.title: Battle of Metemma and Religious Reforms
content: Battle of Metemma (March 9, 1889):
• Yohannis IV faced triple problems: Mahadists, Italians, and disobedient vassals
• Postponed war with Italians to strike Mahadists first
• Ethiopian forces initially successful, but Yohannis was fatally wounded
• Yohannis died the next day, body beheaded by Ansars
Consequences:
• Dynastic shift of power from Tigrayan house to Shewa
• Italians advanced into Mereb Melash region, proclaiming Italian colony of Eritrea (January 1, 1890)
Religious Reforms:
• Yohannis IV attempted religious uniformity
• Council of Borumeda (1878):
- Muslims in Wollo offered choice: convert or lose property
- Some were baptized (e.g., Imam Mohammed Ali became Ras Mikael)
- Orthodoxy: Yohannis ordered all to follow only the Tewahedo doctrine

slides.title: The Battle of Adwa (1896)
content: Background:
• Treaty of Wuchale (May 2, 1889) with Italy
• Article 17: Italian version made Ethiopia a protectorate; Amharic version gave Menilek a choice
• Menilek wrote a circular in 1891 to European governments, proclaiming Ethiopia's position
• February 1893: Menilek unilaterally abrogated Article 17
• June 1894: Ras Mengesha submitted to Menilek, isolating the Italians
Adwa Campaign (1895-1896):
• Three phases:
1. Battle of Ambalage (December 7, 1895)
2. Siege of Mekelle (January 7-21, 1896)
3. Final Battle of Adwa (March 1, 1896)
The Battle:
• Ethiopians from all corners participated
• About 100,000 Ethiopian forces, nearly three-quarters armed with modern rifles
• Italian losses: 7,000 killed, 2,500 wounded, 3,500 prisoners

slides.title: Significance of the Victory of Adwa
content: External Significance:
• Guaranteed Ethiopia's political independence
• Sole independent African country whose independence was recognized
• Restored black dignity and pride in places as far away as South Africa and the US
• Taught Africans a vital lesson: black people are not inferior to white people
• Contributed to the birth of Pan-Africanism, Ethiopianism, Rastafarianism
• Gave powerful impetus to anti-colonial and anti-imperialist struggles
Internal Significance:
• Guaranteed Ethiopia's independence
• Forged Ethiopia's own destiny, free from colonial rule
• Showed if Ethiopians are united, they are strong and invincible
• Enabled Ethiopia to have internationally recognized boundaries:
- Boundary delimitation agreements with French Somaliland (1897)
- With Italian colony of Eritrea (1900, 1902, 1908)
- With Anglo-Egyptian Sudan (1902)
- With British East Africa/Kenya (1907)
- With Italian Somaliland (1908)

slides.title: Religious Reforms and Doctrinal Debates
content: Most Ethiopian Christian monarchs believed religious uniformity would bring national unity.
Yohannis IV's Religious Policy:
• Council of Borumeda (1878):
- Muslims in Wollo: Convert to Orthodox Christianity or lose property
- Imam Mohammed Ali baptized as Ras Mikael
- Imam Amede Liben baptized as Dejach Haile Mariam
Doctrinal Controversies within Ethiopian Orthodox Church:
• Tewahedo (Union): Supported by the Egyptian Patriarch
• Qebat (Unction): Strong support in Gojjam
• Yetsega Lej (Grace): Dominant in Gondar and Shewa
Yohannis IV's Decision:
• Ordered all Orthodox Christians to follow only the Tewahedo doctrine
• Brought an end to doctrinal controversies

slides.title: Power Struggle After Menilek II (1906-1916)
content: 1906: Menilek suffered first stroke; Ras Mekonnen passed away
Measures by Menilek:
• October 1907: Established the first Council of Ministers
• May 1909: Officially designated Lij Iyasu as his legal successor
• Ras Tesema Nadew made regent
Lij Iyasu (1911-1916):
• Tried to give Ethiopian Muslims equal status
• Introduced reforms: auditing government property, municipal police force (Terenbule)
• Established separate Department of Education
• Abolished Quragngna system and Leba Shay (unfair practices)
Reasons for Opposition:
• Religious policy (seen as favoring Islam)
• Polygamy, adultery, contempt for nobility
• Promoted relatives and friends at expense of Shewan nobility
• Antagonized Italy, France, Britain (pro-German/Turkish policy)
• Supported Somali nationalist leader, Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassen
1916 Coup:
• September 27, 1916: Lij Iyasu deposed
• Zewditu named Empress, Dejach Teferi named Ras and heir

slides.title: The Diarchy (1916-1930) and Rise of Haile Selassie
content: Diarchy:
• Zewditu (Empress) and Ras Teferi (heir) theoretically ruled together
• Teferi's power grew progressively, Zewditu became increasingly powerless
Consolidation of Power:
• 1918: Removed all old ministers except Fitawrari Habte Giorgis
• 1926: Abune Matewos and Fitawrari Habte Giorgis passed away (major obstacles removed)
• 1928: Outmaneuvered Dejach Balcha Safo and Dejach Aba Weqaw
• October 1928: Zewditu crowned Teferi as Negus (King of Ethiopia)
Battle of Anchim (March 31, 1930):
• Aircraft used for the first time in Ethiopia for warfare
• Ras Gugsa Wole (Zewditu's husband) defeated and killed
• Two days later, Zewditu died
November 2, 1930: Negus Teferi crowned Emperor Haile Selassie I

slides.title: Italian Aggression (1935-1936)
content: Causes:
• To take revenge for humiliating defeat at Adwa (1896)
• Mussolini's Fascist Party wanted to restore ancient Roman glory
Course of the War:
• October 3, 1935: Italian troops crossed Mereb River
• November 8: Entered Mekelle
• Major Battles: Tembien (January and February 1936), Amba Aradom, Maychew
• March 31, 1936: Battle of Maychew - Ethiopian forces defeated
• May 5, 1936: Italian troops captured Addis Ababa
Southern and Southeastern Fronts:
• Ras Desta Damtew, Dejach Nesibu Zamanuel, Dejach Mekonnen Endalkachew commanded
• Italian forces had complete air control and numerical superiority
League of Nations Response:
• Ethiopia had joined in 1923
• Imposed sanctions on both Ethiopia and Italy (ineffective)
• Emperor Haile Selassie appealed at Geneva, but response was not good

slides.title: Italian Occupation (1936-1941)
content: Occupation:
• Marshal Badoglio first Italian viceroy, then Marshal Rodolfo Graziani
• February 19, 1937: Assassination attempt on Graziani (by Mages Asgedom and Abraha Deboch)
• Tens of thousands of innocent civilians massacred
• Graziani replaced by Duke of Aosta (more liberal)
• Ethiopia became part of Italian East African Empire
Administrative Regions:
1. Eritrea (Asmara)
2. Amhara (Gondar)
3. Oromo-Sidama (Jimma)
4. Addis Ababa/Shewa (Addis Ababa)
5. Harar (Harar)
6. Italian Somaliland (Mogadishu)
Italian Contributions:
• Road building and motor transport expansion
• New urban settlements in major towns
• Electricity, piped water, many factories

slides.title: Patriotic Resistance and Liberation (1936-1941)
content: Two Phases of Resistance:
• Phase 1: Continuation of the Italo-Ethiopian War (conventional fighting)
- Resistance by Ras Desta Damtew, Dejach Beyene Merid, Dejach Gebre Mariam Gari
- Ended with execution of Ras Desta (February 1937)
• Phase 2: Guerrilla warfare (from February 1937 onwards)
Key Figures:
• Abune Petros (spirit behind the offensive, executed)
• Asfawosen Kassa and Abera Kassa (executed after surrender)
Collaborators:
• Ras Hailu Teklehaimanot (main collaborator)
• Ras Seyoum Mengesha, Ras Getachew Abate, others
British Intervention:
• June 1940: Italy entered WWII on Germany's side
• British launched three major offensives from Sudan and Kenya
• April 6, 1941: British forces liberated Addis Ababa
• May 5, 1941: Emperor Haile Selassie returned

presentation_slides.unit_title: Society and Politics in the Age of World Wars, 1914 - 1945

slides.title: UNIT FOUR: Society and Politics in the Age of World Wars, 1914 - 1945
content: This unit covers the major events of the first half of the 20th century.
Key Lessons:
• World War I and its immediate aftermath
• Alliance systems, causes, course, and effects of the war
• Peace settlement
• The Russian Revolution of 1917
• The Inter-War Period (Great Depression and rise of dictators)
• The rise of Fascism and Nazism
• World War II: origins, outbreak, course, and consequences

slides.section: 4.1 World War I and Its Settlement
slides.title: World War I: Alliance Systems
content: World War I (1914-1918): Also known as the Great War, War of the Nations.
Triple Alliance (Central Powers):
• Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy (1879-1882)
• Bismarck's Dual Alliance (Germany-Austria, 1879)
• Expanded to Triple Alliance (1882)
Triple Entente (Allied Powers):
• Britain, France, Russia
• Franco-Russian Alliance (1891-1894)
• Entente Cordiale (Britain-France, 1904)
• Anglo-Russian Entente (1907)
Characteristic:
• The European powers were divided into 'two armed camps'

slides.section: 4.1 World War I and Its Settlement
slides.title: World War I: Causes and Course
content: Crises Leading to War:
• 1908: Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina
• Serbia and Russia forced to accept annexation
• Terrorism by the 'Black Hand' (Death Secret Society in Serbia)
• June 28, 1914: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand (Sarajevo)
- Killed by Bosnian Serb Gavrilo Princip
• July 23, 1914: Austria-Hungary sent ultimatum to Serbia
• July 28, 1914: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia
The War Spreads:
• Russia mobilized to support Serbia
• Germany declared war on Russia, then France
• Britain declared war on Germany (August 4, 1914)
Schlieffen Plan:
• German plan to attack France first through Belgium
• Then turn to fight Russia
• Failed due to British intervention

slides.section: 4.1 World War I and Its Settlement
slides.title: World War I: Major Battles and Technologies
content: Major Theaters:
• Western Front: Germany vs. Allied Powers
• Eastern Front: Germany vs. Russia
Key Battles:
• Mons (Belgium), Tannenberg (Germany)
• Marne (France), Ypres (Belgium)
• Gallipoli (Turkey), Verdun (France)
• Jutland (Denmark), Somme (France), Amiens (France)
New Technologies:
• Chemical warfare (first use)
• Aerial bombardment
• U-boats (submarines)
• Tanks (first use)
Turning Points:
• 1917: Russia withdrew due to the October Revolution (Brest-Litovsk Peace Treaty, March 1918)
• 1917: US entered the war on the side of the Allies

slides.section: 4.1 World War I and Its Settlement
slides.title: World War I: End and Effects
content: End of the War:
• September 29, 1918: Bulgaria signed armistice
• October 30: Ottoman Empire capitulated
• November 3: Austria-Hungary demanded armistice
• November 9: German Republic proclaimed, Kaiser fled
• November 11, 1918: Germany signed armistice (11th hour, 11th day, 11th month)
Effects of the War:
• About 8 million soldiers died
• Nearly three times as many wounded
• Total cost: about $186 billion
Collapse of Empires:
• Russian, German, Austro-Hungarian, and Ottoman empires
Other Consequences:
• Ignited the Russian Revolution
• Laid basis for Cold War
• Laid basis for the rise of National Socialism and WWII

slides.section: 4.1 World War I and Its Settlement
slides.title: The Peace Settlement: Treaties and Terms
content: Major Peace Treaties:
• Treaty of Versailles (Germany, June 1919)
• Treaty of St. Germain (Austria, September 1919)
• Treaty of Trianon (Hungary, June 1920)
• Treaty of Neville (Bulgaria, November 1919)
• Treaty of Sevres (Turkey, August 1920)
The 'Big Three':
• President Wilson (USA)
• Prime Minister Clemenceau (France)
• Prime Minister Lloyd George (UK)
Key Points of Versailles Treaty:
• Germany ceded Alsace-Lorraine to France
• Eupen, Malmedy to Belgium
• Northern Schleswig to Denmark
• Territory lost in the East to Poland ('Polish Corridor')
• Danzig made a 'free city'
• Germany lost 13% of territory, 48% of iron ore, 10% of coal
• Germany's army limited to 100,000
• Germany had to pay reparations (132 billion gold marks)
• Rhineland demilitarized

slides.section: 4.1 World War I and Its Settlement
slides.title: The League of Nations
content: Established: January 1920
Headquarters: Geneva, Switzerland
Primary Goals:
• Prevent wars through collective security and disarmament
• Settle disputes through peaceful means
Membership:
• USA was not a member (Senate refused approval)
• Germany not allowed until 1926
• Russia not a member until 1934
• Dominated by Britain, France, and Italy
Failures:
• Inability to prevent Japanese aggression in Manchuria (1931)
• Inability to prevent Italian aggression in Ethiopia (1935)
Dissolved: 1946 (replaced by the United Nations)

slides.title: The Russian Revolution: Causes and Phases
content: Causes:
• Political: Resented dictatorship of Tsar Nicholas II
• Social: Despotic Tsarist regime oppressed peasants
• Economic: Widespread inflation and famine
• WWI losses further undermined the monarchy
Two Phases:
1. February Revolution (1917): Overthrew Tsar Nicholas II
2. October Revolution (1917): Bolsheviks seized power from the Provisional Government
The Bolsheviks:
• Members of the Russian Social Democratic Labor Party
• Led by Vladimir Lenin
• Organized in a strongly centralized hierarchy
• Refused cooperation with liberal ('bourgeois') groups
The Mensheviks:
• Favored open party membership
• Wanted cooperation with other socialist and non-socialist groups

slides.title: The February and October Revolutions
content: February Revolution (1917):
• Strikes and demonstrations by Petrograd workers
• Petrograd garrison joined the people
• Tsar's government collapsed
• Was a bourgeois revolution
• Made Russia more democratic
October Revolution (1917):
• Lenin returned from exile, adopted 'April Thesis'
• Bolshevik slogan: 'Peace! Bread! Land! All power to the Soviets!'
• October 25, 1917: Nearly bloodless revolt
• Bolsheviks seized power from the Provisional Government
• Based on ideas of Karl Marx
Government Established:
• Soviet Council of People's Commissars
• Lenin as head, Trotsky as commissar of Red Army

slides.title: The Russian Revolution: Aftermath and Significance
content: Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (March 1918):
• Russia made a separate peace with the Central Powers
• Germany dictated the terms
• Russia ceded enormous areas of land, including Ukraine
Significance of the Revolution:
• One of the most important events in modern world history
• Through Communism, Russia served as a model for developing countries
• Fear of Communism spreading to Eastern Europe during the Cold War
• Showed the global impact of the Russian Revolution
Key Figures:
• Vladimir Lenin: Bolshevik leader
• Leon Trotsky: Initially Menshevik, joined Lenin in 1917

slides.section: 4.3 Interwar Period: Capitalist Economy, Fascism and Nazism
slides.title: The Great Depression (1929-1933)
content: The Great Depression:
• Massive global economic recession
• Led to: bank failures, high unemployment, inflation
• Dramatic drops in GDP, industrial production, and stock market prices
Causes:
• Collapse of international trade due to restrictive trade practices
Effects:
• Hit non-industrial countries more harshly
• Prices of raw materials and food fell more sharply than manufactured goods
Political Effects:
• Helped militarists take power in Japan
• Major factor in Hitler's rise to power in Germany (January 1933)
The New Deal (1933-1938):
• Program by President F.D. Roosevelt
• Sought to stimulate the economy and redistribute wealth

slides.section: 4.3 Interwar Period: Capitalist Economy, Fascism and Nazism
slides.title: Fascism: Features and Appeal
content: Origin: 'Fascies' (rods and axes symbolizing authority in ancient Rome)
Features:
• Extreme, aggressive nationalism
• Glorification of strength and military virtues
• Survival of the fittest among nations
• Supreme importance of a national leader (unconditional authority)
• State control of all means of communication
• Tendency towards racism (belief in Aryan superiority)
Appeal of Fascism:
• Attracted petty-bourgeois groups (shopkeepers, entrepreneurs)
• Attracted unemployed people
• Attracted youth and ex-soldiers
• Attracted intellectuals dissatisfied with post-war situation
• Attracted gangsters

slides.section: 4.3 Interwar Period: Capitalist Economy, Fascism and Nazism
slides.title: Rise of Fascism in Italy and Nazism in Germany
content: Italian Fascism:
• Led by Benito Mussolini
• 1919: Organized the Fascist Party
• October 1922: March on Rome
• King Victor Emmanuel III appointed Mussolini as Prime Minister
German Nazism:
• Led by Adolf Hitler
• National Socialist Party (Nazi Party)
• 1923: Attempted to overthrow Weimar Republic (Hitler imprisoned)
• In prison, wrote 'Mein Kampf' (My Struggle)
• January 1933: Hitler became Chancellor
Reasons for Nazi Success:
• German national pride severely harmed by WWI
• Versailles Treaty unpopular
• Economic distress and inflation
• Political discontent against the Weimar Republic

slides.section: 4.3 Interwar Period: Capitalist Economy, Fascism and Nazism
slides.title: Franco's Spain and Japan in the 1930s
content: Franco's Spain:
• General Francisco Franco established right-wing authoritarian regime after Spanish Civil War (1936-1939)
• Received support from Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy
• Was NOT a fascist (had no Fascist ideology, no mass popular movement)
Japan's Regime (1933-1945):
• Sometimes described as 'Fascist'
• Similarities with European Fascism:
- Authoritarianism
- Racism (belief in 'master race')
- Militarism
- Aggressive nationalism
- Hatred of Marxism
• Differences:
- Appeared in a different social and political context
- Was NOT Fascist in the European sense

slides.title: World War II: Alliance Systems and Appeasement
content: Axis Powers:
• Rome-Berlin Axis (1936): Germany and Italy
• Tripartite Pact (September 27, 1940): Germany, Italy, Japan (Rome-Berlin-Tokyo Axis)
Allied Powers:
• Initially: Britain, France, Poland
• Later: USSR, USA, China
Appeasement Policy:
• Britain and France made concessions to Hitler to avoid war
• Reasons: Not ready for war, economic crisis (Depression), US isolationism
Key Events Before the War:
• 1931: Japan took Manchuria
• 1933: Hitler withdrew Germany from League of Nations
• 1936: Hitler militarized the Rhineland
• 1938: Hitler annexed Austria and Sudetenland (Munich Agreement)
• 1939: Italy occupied Albania

slides.title: World War II: Course of the War (1939-1941)
content: Outbreak: September 1, 1939 - Hitler invaded Poland
• Britain and France declared war on Germany (September 3, 1939)
Blitzkrieg (Lightning War):
• Coordinated attacks of air force and fast-moving ground forces
• Germany quickly conquered most of Europe
The Phony War (May 1940):
• No real fighting on the Western Front
• Ended when Germany invaded Denmark, Norway (April 1940)
Fall of France (June 1940):
• Germany invaded Netherlands, Belgium, France (May 10, 1940)
• June 14: Paris surrendered
• Italy declared war on Britain and France (June 10, 1940)
• Vichy France puppet government set up
Battle of Britain (1940):
• Hitler launched attacks from the air
• British used 'Radar' to locate attackers
• Churchill refused to seek peace

slides.title: World War II: Course of the War (1941-1945)
content: Operation Barbarossa (June 22, 1941):
• Germany invaded the Soviet Union
• 'Great Patriotic War' began
• German blitzkrieg failed to bring desired results
• Soviet counterattacks defeated Germans near Moscow
Pearl Harbor (December 7, 1941):
• Japanese surprise attack on US naval base in Hawaii
• US declared war on Japan (December 8, 1941)
• Germany and Italy declared war on US (December 11, 1941)
• Made the war fully a world war
North Africa Campaign:
• 1942: German forces nearly took Egypt
• Late October 1942: British launched major attack
• May 1943: Axis forces in North Africa surrendered

slides.title: World War II: Turning Points and End
content: Invasion of Italy (July 1943):
• King Victor Emmanuel III deposed Mussolini
• Mussolini rescued by German forces
• June 4, 1944: Allied troops occupied Rome
• Mussolini later captured and executed by Italian communists
D-Day (June 6, 1944):
• Operation Overlord - US, British, Canadian forces landed at Normandy
• Major breakthrough in Allied reconquest of Europe
Soviet Advances:
• Operation Bagration (June 22, 1944): Massive Soviet offensive
• By early 1944, Red Army reached border of Poland
End of War in Europe:
• April 30, 1945: Hitler committed suicide
• V-E Day (May 8, 1945) - Germany surrendered

slides.title: World War II: The Pacific Theater and Atomic Bombs
content: Pacific Theater:
• Battle of Midway Island (1942): Decisive defeat for Japanese navy
• By 1944, US forces were getting ready to invade mainland Japan
Yalta Conference (February 1945):
• Churchill, Roosevelt, Stalin met to discuss post-war Europe
• Germany to be divided into American, British, French, and Soviet zones
• Planned for UN establishment
Potsdam Conference (July 1945):
• Agreed on peace settlement with Germany
• Drew up plans for Japan's surrender
Atomic Bombs:
• August 6, 1945: Hiroshima (80,000 killed instantly)
• August 9, 1945: Nagasaki (40,000 killed instantly)
• Death toll rose to about 200,000 from radiation sickness
August 15, 1945: Japan surrendered (V-J Day)

presentation_slides.unit_title: Ethiopia: Internal Developments and External Influences from 1941 to 1991

slides.title: UNIT SIX: Ethiopia: Internal Developments and External Influences from 1941 to 1991
content: This unit covers Ethiopia's history from the restoration of imperial rule to the fall of the Derg in 1991.
Key Topics:
• The Restoration of the Imperial Rule and External Influences
• Socio-economic Conditions and Social Organizations (1941-1974)
• Consolidation of Autocracy and Oppositions to the Monarch
• The 1974 Revolution and the Rise of the Derg
• Socio-economic and Political Reforms of the Military Regime
• The Decline and Downfall of the Derg Regime

slides.section: 6.1 The Restoration of the Imperial Rule and External Influences
slides.title: Restoration of Imperial Rule and British Ascendancy
content: May 1941: Emperor Haile Selassie restored to the throne with British help.
British Ascendancy:
• Britain effectively became the occupying power replacing Italy
• Considerable tension between Ethiopia and Britain
• Ethiopia expected full sovereignty; Britain considered independence a long-term objective
Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement of 1942:
• Confirmed Ethiopia's status as a sovereign state
• But almost every article underlined Ethiopia's dependency on Britain:
- British minister had primacy over all other diplomatic representatives
- British military mission to train the new Ethiopian army
- British citizens occupied key posts (civil and military advisers, police force, financial system)
- Ogaden and strategic areas under British administration

slides.section: 6.1 The Restoration of the Imperial Rule and External Influences
slides.title: The Second Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement and Territorial Issues
content: Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement of 1944:
• Restored some sovereign rights
• British minister's precedence was lifted
• Ethiopian army no longer controlled by British officials
• British agreed to restore parts of the Ethio-Djibouti railway
British Plans for Partition:
• Planned to separate Eritrea and the Ogaden from Ethiopia
• Proposed uniting parts of Tigray with Eritrean highlands (separate Tigrean state)
• Proposed incorporating Ogaden into Greater Somalia
• Envisaged partition of Eritrea, with western lowlands to Sudan
Ethiopia's Response:
• Became a founding member of the UN (1945)
• Made strong demands for both the Ogaden and Eritrea
• British withdrew from parts of Ogaden (1948), restored entire region (1954)

slides.section: 6.1 The Restoration of the Imperial Rule and External Influences
slides.title: The Eritrean Question and Federation
content: Eritrea Under British Administration (1941-1951):
Local Groups in Eritrea:
• Unionist Party: Demanded union with Ethiopia (largest political group)
• Muslim League, Liberal Progressive Party, Pro-Italian Group: Demanded independence
Resolution Process:
• Four Powers Commission (Britain, France, Soviet Union, USA) - could not resolve
• Referred to UN in 1948
• UN Commission (Burma, Guatemala, Norway, Pakistan, South Africa) - divided
UN General Assembly Decision (December 2, 1950):
• Voted for federation with Ethiopia
• Federation came into effect in 1952
• Eritrea became federated with Ethiopia

slides.section: 6.1 The Restoration of the Imperial Rule and External Influences
slides.title: The American Era (1950s-1970s)
content: Following British departure, the US became Ethiopia's main ally.
Kagnew Communications Station Agreement (May 22, 1953):
• US given 25-year lease on the Kagnew station in Asmara
• One of the largest radio relay and communications monitoring stations in the world
• Used to monitor Soviet radio communications
• Named after the first Ethiopian Battalion that fought in the Korean War
US Aid:
• $5 million to equip and train Ethiopian armed forces
• By the 1970s, Ethiopia absorbed 60% of total US military aid to Africa
• Ethiopian armed forces became totally dependent on the US for military hardware
Other US Contributions:
• Ethiopian Air Lines (1945)
• Imperial Highway Authority (1951)
• Education system modeled after the American system
• Peace Corps Program (1960s)

slides.title: Agriculture and Land Tenure System
content: Agriculture:
• Over 60% of GDP and 80% of labor force
• Coffee and agricultural commodities comprised over 90% of exports
• Underdeveloped due to drought, poor infrastructure, government neglect
Land Tenure System (Pre-1974):
Northern Provinces:
• Rist: Communal land ownership based on kinship
• Most peasants held at least some rist land
Southern Provinces:
• Gult: Right to collect tribute from peasants (granted by the state)
• Gabbar System: Peasants reduced to tenants, paying rent and forced labor
Other Forms:
• Samon: Land granted to the Ethiopian Orthodox Church
• Mengist: Government property
• Maderia: Land granted to officials, war veterans, and patriots

slides.title: Land Reform Issues and Agricultural Development
content: Negative Impacts of Feudal Land Tenure:
• Peasants had no security of tenure
• Landowners could evict peasants anytime
• Acceleration of privatization in the south
Land Tax Decrees (1942 onwards):
• Fixed tax based on land classification (lam, lam-taf, taf)
• Used gasha (40 hectares) as measurement
• Faced stiff resistance from landowners
Agricultural Development (Imperial Period):
• Less than 2% of budget allocated to agriculture
• Agricultural production grew below population growth rate
• Commercial agriculture expanded (Tendaho Cotton Plantations, Setiti Humara)
• Minimum Package Program (MPP) introduced (1971)
• Chilalo Agricultural Development Unit (CADU)
Demand for Land Reform:
• Students led 'Land to the Tiller' movement (1965 onwards)
• Land Reform and Development Authority (1965)
• Parliament resisted reforms (landlords represented)
• 1972-74 drought and famine: hundreds of thousands died

slides.title: Trade and Industry
content: Trade:
• Constituted only 7% of GDP in the 1960s
• Coffee was the leading cash crop (50-65% of exports)
• Other exports: hides, skins, pulses, oilseeds
• Major imports: textiles, machinery, chemicals
• Major trading partners: USA (70% of coffee), Italy, Japan
• Balance of trade registered annual deficits (1953-1974)
Industry:
• Less than 5% of GDP in 1975
• Employed only about 60,000 people
Domestic Trade:
• Addis Ababa remained commercial centre (Mercato replaced Arada/Piazza)
• Role of Greek, Armenian, Arab traders challenged by emerging national traders
Development Plans:
• National Economic Council (1954/55)
• First and second five-year plans (1950s-1960s)
• Failed to achieve meaningful results

slides.section: 6.3 Consolidation of Autocracy and Oppositions to the Monarch
slides.title: Haile Selassie's Absolutist Rule (1941-1974)
content: Nature of the State:
• Absolutist state, reaching its height of power
• Top-heavy, secularized bureaucracy
• Imperial myth centered on the Emperor
• Words of the Emperor were final on appointments and decisions
Institutions of Control:
• Military: Army, Imperial Bodyguard, Police Force
• Department of Public Security: Elaborate intelligence network
• Highest budget allocations to Ministry of Defence and Department of Public Security
Administrative Structure:
• 14 provinces (teklay-gizats), each under a governor general
• Sub-divided into awrajas (sub-provinces), weredas (districts), mikitil-weredas (sub-districts)
• High-ranking landed nobles held all important offices
Education System:
• Designed to produce manpower for the bureaucracy
• Haile Selassie I Secondary School (1943), General Wingate School (1946)
• University College of Addis Ababa (1950)
• Haile Selassie I University (1961)

slides.section: 6.3 Consolidation of Autocracy and Oppositions to the Monarch
slides.title: The 1955 Revised Constitution
content: Promulgated on the silver jubilee of the Emperor's coronation.
Reasons for Revision:
• Incorporation of Eritrea (more advanced constitution)
Key Provisions:
• Universal adult suffrage
• Elected Chamber of Deputies (nominal)
• Bicameral parliament (Senate and Chamber of Deputies)
• Senate appointive; Chamber nominally elected
• Low popular participation
Consolidation of Absolutism:
• 'The person of the Emperor is sacred, his dignity is inviolable, and his power is indisputable'
• Human rights provisions accompanied by 'in accordance with the law' or 'within the limits of the law'
Cult of Personality:
• Major landmarks named after the Emperor
• Birth and coronation days celebrated as national holidays

slides.section: 6.3 Consolidation of Autocracy and Oppositions to the Monarch
slides.title: Plots and Conspiracies Against the Emperor
content: Immediate Post-Liberation Groups:
• Returnees (exiles with the Emperor)
• Collaborators (worked with Italians)
• Patriots (played major role in liberation struggle)
Dajjach Belay Zeleke:
• Prominent patriot leader in Gojjam
• Opposed the Emperor as a deserter
• Rejected appointment to southern province
• Surrendered in 1943 after negotiations, but was betrayed
• Broke out of jail, caught, and executed by hanging
Bitwodded Negash Bezabih:
• Famous patriot leader, grandson of Negus Tekle-Haimanot
• Led conspiracy to assassinate Haile Selassie (1951)
• Betrayed by Dajjach Geressu Duki
• Arrested and sentenced to imprisonment
Blatta Takele Wolde-Hawaryat:
• Shewa patriot leader, longest opposition
• Opposed Emperor's return from exile
• Made several attempts to overthrow him
• Killed in shoot-out with police (November 1969)

slides.section: 6.3 Consolidation of Autocracy and Oppositions to the Monarch
slides.title: The 1960 Attempted Coup
content: Leaders: The 'Neway Brothers'
• Brigadier General Mengistu Neway (Commander of the Imperial Bodyguard)
• Germame Neway (the mind/spirit behind the coup)
Supporters:
• Radical intellectuals
• Colonel Worqneh Gebeyehu (Commander of Security Forces)
• Brigadier General Tsege Dibu (Police Force Commander)
Course of Events:
• December 13, 1960: Plotters took hostages at Genete Leul Palace
• Crown Prince Asfawosen appointed as constitutional monarch
• 'People's Government' announced with progressive aristocracy
Demands:
• Improve economic, social, and political problems
Reasons for Failure:
• No attempt to win support of army and air force
• University students supported, but army and air force remained loyal
• Church condemned the coup makers
Outcome:
• Coup suppressed by December 17
• Neway brothers massacred hostages and fled
• Germame committed suicide; Mengistu captured and executed

slides.section: 6.3 Consolidation of Autocracy and Oppositions to the Monarch
slides.title: Peasant Rebellions
content: Common Causes:
• Increasing state pressure on peasant resources
• Ethno-nationalist sentiments
• Land and tax issues
• Maladministration
Woyane Rebellion (Tigray, 1943):
• Led by Blatta Hayle Mariam Redda
• Initial victories, captured Mekelle
• Crushed by imperial forces with British air support
Bale Peasant Rebellion (1963-1970):
• Started in El Kere district
• Local discontent over land and tax issues, opposition to Christian settlement
• Leaders: Kahin Abdi (Somali), Waqo Gutu (Oromo)
• Crushed by massive military operation (1967-1970)
Gojjam Peasant Rebellion (1968):
• Causes: New agricultural income tax, arrogance of governor Tsehayu
• Strong in Motta and Kolla Dega Damot districts
• Government concessions (new tax abandoned, unpopular officials removed)
• Rebellion suppressed by military campaign

slides.section: 6.3 Consolidation of Autocracy and Oppositions to the Monarch
slides.title: Armed Struggle in Eritrea and Other Movements
content: Eritrean Armed Struggle:
• Federation came into effect (1952), but imperial government wanted direct rule
• 1962: Eritrea became the 14th province of Ethiopia
Separatist Movements:
• Eritrean Liberation Movement (ELM, 1958) - discovered and disbanded
• Eritrean Liberation Front (ELF, 1960) - launched armed struggle (1961)
- Supported by radical Arab states (Egypt, Syria, Iraq)
- Dominated by Muslims, later split into three groups
• Eritrean People's Liberation Forces (EPLF, 1972) - formed from splinter groups
Mecha-Tulama Self-Help Association (1963):
• Promoted Oromo self-identity
• Provided education, water supply, communication, health facilities
• Became politically active, considered a threat
• Brigadier General Taddesse Birru (elected president) arrested (1966)
• Banned (1966), led to rise of more militant Oromo nationalism

slides.section: 6.3 Consolidation of Autocracy and Oppositions to the Monarch
slides.title: The Ethiopian Student Movement
content: Causes: Expansion of secondary and higher education
Phases of the Movement:
Phase 1 (1950s):
• Demanded improvement in learning facilities and services
• Student councils as organizations
Phase 2 (After 1960):
• More radical demands
• Influenced by the 1960 coup, Eritrean resistance
Phase 3 (Mid-1960s onwards):
• Revolutionary phase
• Birth of 'crocodiles' (radical core, Marxist ideas)
• February 1965: Demonstration against feudal land tenure ('Land to the Tiller!')
• 1969: Raised issue of rights of nations and nationalities
Student Organizations:
• University Students' Union of Addis Ababa (USUAA) - Tagel
• Ethiopian Students' Union in North America (ESUNA) - Challenge
• Ethiopian Students' Union in Europe (ESUE) - Tataq
Confrontation: December 28, 1969 - Tilahun Gizaw killed, violence escalated

slides.section: 6.4 The 1974 Revolution: The Downfall of the Emperor and the Rise of the Derg
slides.title: The 1974 Revolution: Causes and Popular Upsurge
content: Causes of the Revolution:
• Failure to effect significant economic and political reforms
• Rising inflation and corruption
• Famine affecting several provinces (especially Wollo)
The Popular Upsurge (January-June 1974):
January 1974: Negele-Borena Mutiny
• Fourth Brigade mutinied over provisions (food, water)
• Took commanding officers hostage
• Concessions made to mutineers encouraged spread of discontent
February 18, 1974: Revolution reached Addis Ababa
• Teachers went on strike (opposed Sector Review, demanded higher pay)
• University students joined demonstrations
• Taxi drivers struck against fuel price increases
Military Mutiny Spreads:
• Second Division (Asmara), Fourth Division (Addis Ababa), Air Force (Dabra Zayt) mutinied
• Soldiers demanded salary increases and political reforms
• Formed Coordinating Committee of the Armed Forces (precursor of the Derg)

slides.section: 6.4 The 1974 Revolution: The Downfall of the Emperor and the Rise of the Derg
slides.title: The Revolution Intensifies (April-June 1974)
content: Government Responses:
• February 1974: Akllu Habte Wold and cabinet forced to resign
• March 1974: Endalkachew Mekonnen appointed Prime Minister
• Promised reforms (constitutional reform)
• Allowed army significant salary increase
March 1974: General Strike
• Confederation of Ethiopian Labor Unions (CELU) staged successful general strike
• Paralyzed the entire nation, especially the capital
April 20, 1974: Muslim Demonstrations
• Estimated 100,000 Muslims and Christian sympathizers
• Demanded religious equality
April-May 1974: Coordinating Committee Actions
• Colonel Alem Zewd Tessema (chairman) arrested former officials
• But failed to contain unrest
• Endalkachew replaced committee with High National Security Commission
June 28, 1974: The Derg Formed
• 120 members from every military and police unit
• Major Mengistu Haile Mariam as chairman
• Major Atnafu Abate as vice-chairman

slides.section: 6.4 The 1974 Revolution: The Downfall of the Emperor and the Rise of the Derg
slides.title: The Derg Takes Control and Deposes the Emperor
content: The 'Creeping Coup' (June 28 - September 12, 1974):
• Derg professed loyalty to the Emperor
• Began arresting members of the aristocracy and high-ranking officials
• Forced out Prime Minister Endalkachew, replaced by Lij Mikael Imru
Derg's Motto: 'Ethiopia Tikdem' (Ethiopia First)
Deposition of the Emperor (September 12, 1974):
• Proclamation officially deposed Haile Selassie
• Suspended the Revised Constitution of 1955
• Dissolved Parliament
• Established Provisional Military Administrative Council (PMAC)
• General Aman Andom appointed Head of State
General Aman Andom's Challenges:
• Disagreed with Derg on three issues:
- Size of the Derg (too large)
- Eritrean insurgency (urged reconciliation)
- Fate of political prisoners (opposed death penalty)

slides.section: 6.4 The 1974 Revolution: The Downfall of the Emperor and the Rise of the Derg
slides.title: Bloody Saturday and Consolidation of Power
content: October 7, 1974: Derg crushed civilian dissidents
November 23, 1974: Bloody Saturday
• General Aman Andom killed while resisting arrest
• 52 senior officials of the old regime executed
• About half a dozen leaders of military units opposing Derg executed
• Total of 60 victims (known as the 'sixty')
Significance of Bloody Saturday:
• Most damaging political blunder of the Derg
• Discredited the regime both at home and abroad
• Eliminated all moderate opposition
After Bloody Saturday:
• Brigadier General Tafari Banti became Chairman of PMAC and Head of State (November 28, 1974)
• Major Mengistu retained power as First Vice-Chairman
• Mengistu emerged as the decisive force in the Derg

slides.section: 6.5 Socio-economic and Political Reforms of the Military Regime
slides.title: Early Reforms: Zemecha and Land Reform
content: Development through Cooperation Campaign (Zemecha):
• Announced October 1974, launched December 1974
• Aimed to mobilize university and secondary students to the countryside
• Explain socialist revolution and land reform to peasants
• Improve literacy rate
• Terminated June 1976 (EPRP members infiltrated and incited opposition)
Other Zemecha Campaigns:
• Yearnguadew Zemecha (Green Campaign, 1978) - rapid economic development
• Yemesrettimhirt Zemecha (Literacy Campaign, 1979) - some success
• Yeqeyi Kokeb Zemecha (Red Star Campaign, 1982) - solve Eritrean problem
Proclamation of Ethiopian Socialism:
• Changed slogan from 'Ethiopia Tikdem' to 'Ethiopian Socialism'
• March 1975: All royal titles revoked, proposed constitutional monarchy abandoned

slides.section: 6.5 Socio-economic and Political Reforms of the Military Regime
slides.title: Radical Economic Reforms (1975)
content: Nationalization of Rural Land (March 1975):
• Abolished all private land ownership
• Set ceiling on family holdings at ten hectares
• Provided for formation of peasant associations (village, district, provincial levels)
• Peasant associations in charge of implementation in cooperation with Zemecha
Nationalization of Urban Land and Extra Houses (1975):
• All urban land and rentable dwellings nationalized
• Kebeles established as basic unit of urban government
• Served as instruments of socio-political control
Impact:
• Dismantled socio-economic basis of feudo-capitalism
• Replaced by a socialist socio-economic order
• Both rural and urban communities organized into hierarchy of associations

slides.section: 6.5 Socio-economic and Political Reforms of the Military Regime
slides.title: Political Organizations and Party Formation
content: Marxist-Leninist Organizations Emerge:
• Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Party (EPRP / Ehapa)
• All-Ethiopian Socialist Movement (Meison)
• Workers' League (Wezlig)
• Ethiopian Marxist-Leninist Organization (Malerid)
• Ethiopian Oppressed Masses Revolutionary Struggle (Echa'at)
• Abyotaw Seded (Revolutionary Flame - launched by Mengistu)
Union of Marxist-Leninist Organizations (Emaledih - early 1977):
• Task: Identify strategies for creating a vanguard party
• Meison left the union (leaders killed or arrested)
• Other members (Echa'at, Wezlig, Malerid) expelled
Commission for Organizing the Party of the Workers of Ethiopia (COPEW - December 1979):
• Mengistu as chairman
• Workers' Party of Ethiopia (WPE) proclaimed (September 12, 1984)
• Mengistu became first secretary-general

slides.section: 6.5 Socio-economic and Political Reforms of the Military Regime
slides.title: Mass Organizations and the PDRE
content: Mass Organizations Created:
• All-Ethiopia Trade Union (AETU) - replaced CELU (1977)
• All-Ethiopia Peasants' Association (AEPA) / Ethiopian Peasants' Association (EPA)
• Revolutionary Ethiopian Women's Association (REWA - 1980)
• Revolutionary Ethiopian Youth Association (REYA - 1980)
People's Democratic Republic of Ethiopia (PDRE - September 1987):
• Institute for the Study of Nationalities established
• Constitution drafted and ratified by 'referendum' (February 1987)
• National Shengo (supreme body) elected
• Mengistu became the country's first civilian president
• Still remained WPE's general secretary
Nature of the Regime:
• Members of the now-defunct Derg still ran the government
• Same people with different titles

slides.section: 6.5 Socio-economic and Political Reforms of the Military Regime
slides.title: Resettlement and Villagization Policies
content: 1984/85 Famine:
• More severe than 1973/74 famine
• Affected nearly eight million people, killed about one million
• Clear manifestation of failure of regime's economic policy
Resettlement Policy:
• Permanent relocation of about 1.5 million people from north to south/southwest
• Rationale: Combat drought, avert famine, increase agricultural productivity
• Critics: Poorly planned, haphazardly executed, forceful relocation
• Thousands died from malaria and sleeping sickness
• 100,000 people died under the program
• Suspicions: Primary motive was to depopulate northern insurgency areas
Villagization Program (January 1985):
• Relocation of peasants into larger villages (40-300 families)
• Rationale: Better access to services, efficient resource use, hasten collectivization
• Critics: Impoverished peasants, reduced productive capacity, population control
• Services not delivered as promised

slides.section: 6.6 The Decline and Downfall of the Derg Regime
slides.title: Internal Challenges and Power Struggles (1976-1977)
content: Major Challenges Facing the PMAC (1976-1977):
• Power struggle within the Derg
• EPRP attacked the Derg, demanding power transfer to civilian government
• Eritrean insurgents (ELF, EPLF) - encircled Asmara
• Ethiopian Democratic Union (EDU) - advancing from Sudan
• Somalia invaded Ethiopia (Ogaden War, 1977)
Power Struggle within the Derg:
• Summer 1976: Mengistu eliminated powerful members (Sisay Habte, Getachew Nadew, others)
• February 3, 1977: Palace coup - Colonel Daniel Asfaw arrested General Tafari Benti and others
• All key members of the PMAC were taken away and executed
• Mengistu declared himself the Derg's chairman
• November 1977: Atnafu Abaate eliminated - Mengistu in undisputed command

slides.section: 6.6 The Decline and Downfall of the Derg Regime
slides.title: The White Terror and Red Terror
content: White Terror (EPRP):
• Urban guerrilla warfare by EPRP against the Derg
• Assassinations of Derg supporters
• Attempt on Colonel Mengistu's life (September 23, 1976)
Red Terror (Derg):
• Government security forces systematically hunted down suspected EPRP members
• Between 1977 and 1978: Estimated 100,000 people killed or disappeared
• Targeted 'reactionaries' and 'anarchists' (anyone opposing the regime)
Results of the Red Terror:
• Destroyed all civilian opposition groups mercilessly
• Uprooted EPRP from all cities and towns
• Split within EPRP hastened its collapse
• Surviving members retreated to the countryside to form Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Army (EPRA)

slides.section: 6.6 The Decline and Downfall of the Derg Regime
slides.title: The Ogaden War (1977-1978)
content: Background:
• Somalia's irredentist ambition to annex the Ogaden
• Somali President Siad Barre saw the Derg's problems as opportunity to attack
Course of the War:
• Somalia launched full-scale invasion
• Ethiopian forces outnumbered in manpower and weapons, forced to retreat
• Within months, Somali forces captured large parts of the Ogaden, threatened Harar and Dire Dawa
Ethiopian Response:
• PMAC issued general mobilization
• Massive response from Ethiopian people, rallying behind the PMAC
• About 100,000 peasant militia trained at Tateq Training Camp
• Ethiopians launched counter-offensive, routed Somali invaders in weeks
External Support:
• Soviet Union, Cuba, and Democratic Republic of Yemen supported Ethiopia
• Ethiopia received Russian weapons and Cuban troops
• Somalia expelled Soviets and broke diplomatic relations
Outcome:
• Major realignment of power in the Horn of Africa
• Ethiopia broke off relations with the US completely
• Soviet Union became Ethiopia's primary ally

slides.section: 6.6 The Decline and Downfall of the Derg Regime
slides.title: The Derg and the Armed Struggle in Eritrea
