content: After the Ogaden War: PMAC turned against Eritrean secessionists.
Initial Success:
• Massive human and material resources deployed
• Substantial gains in rural areas, secessionists forced to pull back
• Major towns captured, road from Addis Ababa to Asmara opened
EPLF Response:
• Sustained heavy losses but survived
• Regrouped in the Naqfa area
• Government failed to dislodge the EPLF from Naqfa
Turning Point:
• 1988: Afabet fell to the EPLF (major defeat for the Derg)
• 1990: Massawa captured by EPLF
• Decisive blow to the government army

slides.section: 6.6 The Decline and Downfall of the Derg Regime
slides.title: The Northern Insurgency and Downfall of the Derg
content: Soviet Policy Changes (Late 1980s):
• Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika
• Reduced military assistance to Ethiopia
• Collapse of the Soviet Union (1991)
• US became the sole undisputed global power
TPLF Advances:
• History traced back to 1975
• Mid-1980s: Consolidated, repulsed Derg offensives
• Captured several small towns in Tigray
• February 1989: Captured Enda Sellase
EPRDF Formation:
• TPLF abandoned initial objective of Tigray republic
• Merged with other groups to form Ethiopian Peoples' Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF)
• Founding members: TPLF, EPDM, OPDO, EDORM
Final Phase:
• March 1988: Nadew Command routed by EPLF
• May 1989: Aborted coup attempt; top generals arrested and executed
• 1990-1991: EPRDF advanced into Gondar, Gojjam, Wollo, Shewa
• May 21, 1991: Mengistu fled to Harare, Zimbabwe
• May 28, 1991: EPRDF forces entered Addis Ababa
• EPLF took complete control of Eritrea (de facto independence)

slides.title: UNIT SEVEN: Africa since the 1960s
content: This unit covers the main historical developments in Africa since the 1960s.
Key Topics:
• The Road to Independence and the Rise of Independent States
• Politics in Independent African States
• Economy and Society in Independent Africa
• The Cold War and Africa
• Pan-Africanism and the Transition from OAU to AU

slides.title: The Road to Independence in Africa
content: National liberation movements took two courses: violent and non-violent.
West African Independence (Peaceful):
• No significant number of white settlers
• Long history of nationalist movements
British West Africa:
• Gold Coast (Ghana) - led by Kwame Nkrumah - independent March 1957
• Nigeria - led by Nnamdi Azikwe - independent October 1960
• Sierra Leone - independent April 1961
• Gambia - independent February 1964
French West Africa:
• 1958: de Gaulle offered choice between autonomy (within French Community) or independence
• Guinea voted 'No' - independent 1958 (first)
• Other colonies voted 'Yes' initially
• By November 1960, all French West African colonies achieved full independence

slides.title: The 'Africa Year' (1960) and Settler Colonialism
content: Africa Year (1960):
• Seventeen French colonies achieved independence
• Cameroon, Togo, Dahomey, Niger, Upper Volta, Ivory Coast, Chad
• Ubangi Shari, Middle Congo, Gabon, Senegal, French Sudan, Mauritania
Settler Colonies (Violent Independence):
• Significant number of white settlers made independence difficult
Algerian War of Independence (1954-1962):
• Algeria had been a French colony since 1830
• About one million white settlers (colons)
• Leaders: Ben Bella and the National Liberation Front (FLN)
• January 1961: Referendum, 75% voted for independence
• Evian Agreement (March 18, 1962) - ended the war
• July 1, 1962: Algeria became independent
• Ben Bella became first President

slides.title: Politics in Independent African States
content: Post-independence African states faced political instability.
Military Coups:
• Most frequent means of changing government in 1960s-1980s
• Coup followed coup in Togo, Dahomey (Benin)
• Nigeria and Ghana experienced coups (1966)
Reasons for Military Involvement:
• Legacy of colonial rule
• Corruption in civilian regimes
• Military seen as disciplined and free from corruption
Examples of Tyrannical Rulers:
• General 'Emperor' Jean Bedel Bokassa (Central African Republic)
• Field Marshal Idi Amin (Uganda) - killed thousands, looted the economy
• Francisco Macias Nguema (Equatorial Guinea) - killed/thousands died
Nigeria:
• Civil war (1967-70) over Biafra secession
• General Gowon achieved post-war reconciliation
• 1975: General Murtala Muhammed overthrew Gowon, set timetable for civilian rule
• 1976: Muhammed assassinated, General Obasanjo took power, returned to civilian rule (1979)

slides.title: Ghana's Political Instability
content: 1966: Kwame Nkrumah overthrown
• Blamed for prioritizing external affairs over domestic problems
• Forced into exile in Guinea
1972: Colonel Ignatius Acheampong staged coup
• 'Operation Feed Yourself' - aimed at reducing food imports
• Unable to halt overall economic decline
1979: Flight Lieutenant Jerry Rawlings seized power
• Three former military heads executed for corruption
• Returned to civilian rule within three months
December 1981: Rawlings seized power again
• Proclaimed a 'people's revolution'
• Removed old political elites from power

slides.section: 7.3 Economy and Society in Independent Africa
slides.title: Economy and Society in Independent Africa
content: Major Problem: Lack of economic diversity
Colonial Legacy:
• Africans encouraged to produce raw materials only
• Little effort to establish factories
• Specialization in single cash-crop products
• Unstable prices in world markets
Economic Crisis:
• International debt and drought (1980s-1990s)
• 22 countries could not feed their populations (1985)
• Agricultural production declined in early 1980s
Positive Examples:
• Botswana, Algeria, Gabon, Cote d'Ivoire recorded substantial achievements
Political Legacy:
• Colonial misrule had great impact on development
• Struggles for economic independence continued

slides.title: The Cold War in Africa
content: Africa was a hotspot for Cold War rivalry between USA and USSR.
Soviet Involvement:
• Clear anti-imperialist ideology
• Gamal Abdel Nasser (Egypt) - first to seek Soviet support (Suez Crisis, 1956)
• Sekou Toure (Guinea) - turned to Soviets after French expulsion
• Soviet support for Mali, Ghana, Algeria
• By 1970s, Soviet Union became leading arms dealer in sub-Saharan Africa
• From $2 million (1974) to $3.4 billion (1979) in arms sales
US Involvement:
• Initially deferred to European allies
• Ethiopia (1953-1977): Major recipient of US aid
• After Derg came to power, US supported Somalia
• Egypt: Under Sadat, received US support after Yom Kippur War (1973)
• Libya: Bad relations with US (Gaddafi's hostility to Israel, support for terrorism)

slides.title: Settler Colonialism: Mozambique, Angola, and Zimbabwe
content: Portuguese Colonies:
• Angola and Mozambique had significant white settlers
• Liberation struggles started in early 1960s
Angola:
• Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA) - led by Agostino Neto
• 1975: Portuguese withdrawal, power struggle with UNITA
• MPLA government established, but continued civil war
Mozambique:
• Front for the Liberation of Mozambique (FRELIMO) - led by Eduardo Mondlane, then Samora Machel
• 1975: Mozambique gained independence
Zimbabwe (Southern Rhodesia):
• White minority government (1970: declared a republic)
• ZANU (Robert Mugabe) and ZAPU (Joshua Nkomo) fought liberation war
• 1979: Internal settlement, adopted name Zimbabwe
• April 18, 1980: Internationally recognized independence
• Mugabe became first Prime Minister

slides.title: The End of Apartheid in South Africa
content: Apartheid System (1948-early 1990s):
• Institutionalized racial segregation and discrimination
• Afrikaner National Party won 1948 election, strengthened segregation
Key Laws:
• Population Registration Act (1950): Classified people by race
• Group Areas Act (1950): Designated residential areas by race
• Bantu Education Act (1953): Prevented black South Africans from quality education
Resistance Movements:
• African National Congress (ANC) - founded 1912
• Leaders: Nelson Mandela, Oliver Tambo, Walter Sisulu
• March 21, 1960: Sharpeville Massacre (69 killed, 180 wounded)
Turning Points:
• ANC and PAC banned (1960)
• ANC established armed wing (Umkhonto we Sizwe)
• 1963: Mandela and others sentenced to life imprisonment
International Response:
• UN condemned apartheid, but sanctions blocked by UK and US (veto)
• South Africa withdrew from Commonwealth (1961)
End of Apartheid:
• 1970s: Black Consciousness movement
• 1980s: Mass protests, boycotts, strikes
• 1990: Nelson Mandela released
• 1994: First democratic elections - Mandela became President

slides.title: Pan-Africanism and the Organization of African Unity (OAU)
content: Pan-Africanism:
• Expression of desire for African unity and unity of all black peoples
• Originated in the Americas (Afro-Americans, Caribbean)
• Early leaders: W.E.B. Du Bois (Father of Pan-Africanism), Marcus Garvey (Back to Africa Movement)
Pan-African Conferences:
• First: London (1900) - organized by H. Sylvester Williams
• Five conferences before 1945
• Fifth: Manchester (1945) - landmark (African leaders participated)
- Demanded African independence
- Participants: Kwame Nkrumah, Jomo Kenyatta
Organization of African Unity (OAU):
• Founded May 1963 in Addis Ababa
• 32 African states signed the charter
• Primary aims:
- Coordinate and intensify cooperation
- Defend sovereignty, territorial integrity, and independence
- Eradicate all forms of colonialism and white minority rule

slides.title: The OAU: Successes, Failures, and Transition to AU
content: Two Opposing Blocs:
• Casablanca Group: Immediate political union (Ghana, Algeria, Guinea, Morocco, Egypt, Mali, Libya)
• Monrovia Group: Gradual economic integration first (Ethiopia, Nigeria, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Togo, Tunisia, Congo Kinshasa, Somalia)
Emperor Haile Selassie's Role:
• Bridged the gap between the two groups
• Invited leaders to Addis Ababa
• Succeeded in creating the OAU in 1963
OAU Achievements:
• Helped African countries achieve independence
• Supported anti-apartheid and liberation struggles
• African Development Bank established
OAU Failures:
• Criticized as 'Dictators' Club' or 'Dictator's Trade Union'
• No military wing to enforce decisions
• Policy of non-interference (could not stop civil wars)
• Could not condemn human rights violations by member states
African Union (AU):
• Sirte Declaration (September 1999) - called for new organization
• Inaugurated July 2002 in Durban, South Africa
• Stronger focus on economic and political integration
• Established Peace and Security Council, Pan-African Parliament, Human Rights institutions

slides.title: UNIT EIGHT: Post 1991 Developments in Ethiopia
content: This unit covers Ethiopia's history after the fall of the Derg in 1991.
Key Topics:
• The Transitional Government of Ethiopia (1991-1995)
• The Formation of FDRE and the 1995 Constitution
• Ethiopia after the 1995 Constitution
• Socio-Economic Issues
• The Role of Ethiopia in Peacekeeping

slides.title: The Transitional Government (1991-1995)
content: Establishment:
• June 28, 1991: Derg regime overthrown
• EPRDF facilitated the establishment of Transitional Government of Ethiopia (TGE)
• National Conference in Addis Ababa (June 1991)
• 'Transitional Period Charter' adopted
Key Changes:
• New ethnic and language-based administrative structure
• 14 regions replaced previous 14 geographic provinces
• Former Ethiopian Armed Forces dismantled
• Ex-soldiers demobilized and became jobless
Drafting the Constitution:
• Constituent Assembly established
• Draft constitution presented for 'public discussion'
• Constitution of FDRE endorsed in August 1995

slides.title: The 1995 Constitution and Political Developments
content: Key Features of the 1995 Constitution:
• Recognized human and democratic rights
• Recognized international regional declarations on human rights
• Recognized rights of nations, nationalities, and peoples for self-determination
Article 39 (Controversial):
• 'Every Ethiopian Nation, Nationality and people has an unconditional right to self-determination'
• 'Every Nation, Nationality and People has the right to a full measure of self-government'
• Critics argue this encourages secession and is dangerous for the country's survival
Federal Structure:
• 9 regions and 2 city states (Addis Ababa, Dire Dawa)
• Later: Sidama and Southwestern Ethiopian regional states added
• Based on language and ethnicity
Political Ideology:
• Revolutionary Democracy - ideology of the EPRDF-led government
• Economy based on agriculture

slides.title: National Elections Under the FDRE
content: Elections Conducted: 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015
1995 Election:
• Some parties boycotted (All-Amhara Peoples' Organization, etc.)
• EPRDF won majority and formed government
2000 Election:
• Many parties participated (including those who boycotted previously)
• EPRDF again claimed landslide victory
2005 Election (Most Significant):
• Opposition parties united and better organized
• Coalition for Unity and Democracy (CUD) formed
• 90% voter turnout reported
• CUD won 180 seats (all 23 seats in Addis Ababa)
• NEBE declared EPRDF won 50%+1 vote
• Opposition rejected results
• Protests led to deaths and arrests
• CUD leaders sentenced to life imprisonment (later pardoned)
2010 and 2015 Elections:
• Less optimism
• EPRDF claimed majority of seats

slides.title: The Ethio-Eritrean War (1998-2000)
content: Causes: Boundary dispute over Badme
Course of the War:
• May 6, 1998: Eritrean forces attacked Badme
• May 13, 1998: Ethiopian forces launched counter-offensive
International Mediation:
• USA and Rwanda proposed peace plan (evacuation of Eritrean troops)
• Eritrea rejected, called for demilitarization and direct talks
Operation Sunset (February 22, 1999):
• Ethiopia launched massive military offensive
• Recaptured most contested territories (Badme, Zalambessa)
• May 25, 1999: Ethiopia declared the war over
Casualties: Tens of thousands killed on both sides
Algiers Agreement (June 18, 2000):
• Comprehensive peace agreement signed
• 25km Temporary Security Zone (TSZ) established
• UNMEE deployed to patrol the zone
Boundary Commission Ruling (April 13, 2002):
• Awarded Badme to Eritrea
• Ethiopia requested further explanation, didn't implement decision
• 'No peace no war' situation for over a decade
Resolution:
• Relations improved after Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power

slides.title: Socio-Economic Developments Under the EPRDF
content: Economic Policy Shift:
• From command economy to market-oriented economy
• Capital limit for private investors lifted
• Government still participated in the economy
Land Issue:
• Land remained state property
• No private ownership of land
Agriculture:
• Agricultural Development-Led Industrialization (ADLI)
• Fertilizers and improved seeds increased yields
• Agricultural extension workers trained in large numbers
• Model peasants rewarded
Infrastructure Development:
• Road infrastructure and education: top budget sectors
• Universal Electrification Access Program (UEAP)
• Telecommunications infrastructure expanded
Great Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD):
• Foundation stone laid (2011) by Prime Minister Meles Zenawi
• Capacity: 6000 Mega Watts
• Financed by Ethiopian people (bonds)
• Source of tension with Egypt and Sudan over Nile water rights
• Ethiopia not a signatory to 1929 and 1959 Nile treaties

slides.section: 8.4 The Role of Ethiopia in Peacekeeping
slides.title: Ethiopia's Role in Peacekeeping and Counter-Terrorism
content: UN Peacekeeping Missions:
• Long history dating back to the 1950s
• Korea, Congo, Rwanda, Burundi, Liberia, Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia
• Currently 8,297 troops, police, and military experts deployed
AU Peacekeeping:
• African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM)
• 4,395 uniformed personnel to the operation
Fighting Terrorism:
• Active participation in combating terrorism
• Worked to prevent Somalia from becoming a safe haven
• Collaborated with international community (especially US)
• Launched punitive military campaigns within Somalia
• Targeted Al-Shabaab terrorist group

presentation_slides.unit_title: Indigenous Knowledge Systems and Heritages of Ethiopia

slides.title: UNIT NINE: Indigenous Knowledge Systems and Heritages of Ethiopia
content: This unit covers Ethiopia's indigenous knowledge systems and historical heritage.
Key Topics:
• Definition and unique characteristic features of indigenous knowledge
• Indigenous knowledge and development
• Ethiopia's indigenous knowledge systems
• Heritages of Ethiopia (tangible and intangible)
• Festivals and cultural practices
• UNESCO-registered heritage sites

slides.title: Indigenous Knowledge: Definition and Characteristics
content: Definition:
• Knowledge systems and practices developed outside the formal educational system
• Based on centuries of experimentation to cope with agro-ecological and socio-economic environments
• Also called traditional knowledge, local knowledge, folk knowledge
Unique Characteristics:
1. Local: Rooted in a particular place
2. Adaptive: Based on historical experiences, adapts to change
3. Cumulative: Developed from centuries of living in proximity to nature
4. Holistic: All aspects of life are interconnected
5. Humble: Lives in harmony with nature, not controlling it
6. Intergenerational: Passed from one generation to the next
7. Invaluable: Key to sustainable social and economic development
8. Irreplaceable: Cannot be replicated by western science
9. Moral: Has a right and wrong way to interact with nature
10. Relative: Knowledge varies by age and experience
11. Responsible: Responsibility for well-being of the environment
12. Spiritual: Rooted in social and spiritual relations
13. Valid: Does not require validation by western science

slides.title: Ethiopia's Indigenous Knowledge Systems
content: Ethiopia is rich in diverse indigenous knowledge systems in various areas.
Agriculture:
• Traditional farming techniques, terracing (Konso)
Architecture:
• Obelisk of Aksum, rock-hewn churches of Lalibela, castles of Gondar
• Wall of Harar
Medicine:
• Medicinal properties of many plants discovered
Cottage Industry:
• Iron smelting, tanning, weaving
Philosophy:
• Rich in oral and written philosophical literature (Ge'ez, Arabic)
• Proverbs, songs, folktales
Conflict Resolution:
• Traditional methods of conflict resolution
Examples:
• Gada system (Oromo) - indigenous democratic socio-political system
• Dagu system (Afar) - unique information exchange system ('Internet of the Afar')
• Luwa system (Sidama) - generational class system

slides.title: Heritages of Ethiopia: Definition and Types
content: Heritage Definition:
• Legacy of physical artifacts and intangible attributes inherited from past generations
• Both material and non-material culture
Values of Heritages:
• Promote interpretation of the past
• Commemorative value (collective memory and identity)
• Symbol of nationalism and national identity
• Instruments for nation-building
Types of Heritages:
Cultural Heritage:
• Tangible Cultural Heritage:
- Movable: Manuscripts, paintings, sculptures, inscriptions
- Immovable: Buildings, monuments, archaeological remains, palaces
• Intangible Cultural Heritage:
- Performances, ceremonies, music, drama, literature
- Religious, wedding, mourning ceremonies
Natural Heritage:
• National parks, gardens, mountain chains, natural areas

slides.title: Examples of Ethiopian Heritages
content: Literature (Ge'ez):
• Dominated by the Bible and Christian liturgy
• Hagiographies, literature about indigenous Ethiopian saints
• Works of history, ecclesiastical and civil law, philology, medicine
• Significant collections found outside Ethiopia (UK, France, Italy, Germany, US)
Al Nejashi Mosque:
• Oldest mosque in Ethiopia (Tigray)
• Established after the first followers of Prophet Mohammed sought refuge in Aksum (615 AD)
• King Ella Sham (Negash) granted them asylum
Palaces:
• Jimma Abba Jifar's Palace (18th century) - influenced by Indian architecture
• Kumsa Moreda's Palace (Wollega, 1870s)
• Sheikh Hojele's Residence (Addis Ababa)
Halala Kella (Dawuro):
• Defensive dry stone walls and ditches (16th-18th centuries)
• Built to protect against invaders
• Estimated length: 1,000 km total

slides.title: Archaeological Sites and Art
content: Archaeological Sites:
• Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis) - named after Afar region
• Melka Kunture prehistoric site
• Tiya erected stones
• Awash and Omo valleys
• Hadar region (Afar)
• Fincha Habera site (Bale Mountains) - 30,000-year-old rock shelter (highest altitude human occupation)
Ethiopian Art:
• Christian art (paintings, crosses, icons, illuminated manuscripts)
• Lalibela Cross (12th century)
• Popular arts: textiles, basketry, jewelry
• Islamic illuminated manuscripts (Harar)
• Modern artists: Afework Tekle, Eskender Bogosian, Gebrekristos Desta, Agegnehu Engida
Music:
• Azmaris (wandering musicians)
• Yared - said to have invented musical notation
• Four major melodies: Bati, Tizeta, Ambassel, Anchihoye (gifts of Wollo)
• Modern music: 1960s-70s - Tilahun Gessesse, Ali Birra, Mahmoud Ahmed

slides.title: Festivals of Ethiopia
content: Ashenda/Ashendiye/Solel:
• Celebrated in Tigray, Amhara, Agaw (August 16-26)
• Commemorates ascension of Virgin Mary
• Girls wear distinctive grass (Ashenda) around their waists
• Door-to-door celebrations, dancing, gifts
Timket (Ethiopian Epiphany):
• Commemorates baptism of Jesus (January 18-19)
• Ketera: Blocking water for blessing
• Tabots (replicas of Ark of the Covenant) processed
Meskel (Founding of the True Cross):
• Celebrated September 26
• Demera bonfire - decorated with Adey Abeba flowers
• Registered by UNESCO as World Heritage (September 2019)
Irreecha (Oromo Thanksgiving):
• Celebrated at beginning of spring (Birraa)
• At sacred lakes (Hora Harsadi, Bishoftu)
• Thanks Waaqa (God) for plentiful harvest
Fiche Chambalalla (Sidama New Year):
• Registered by UNESCO as World Heritage (September 2019)
• Communal events, traditional songs and dances
• Enhances equity, good governance, social cohesion
Gifaataa (Wolaita New Year Festival):
• Celebrates end of rainy season and beginning of warm season
• Peace-making and conflict resolution

slides.title: Egalitarian Democracies and Indigenous Institutions
content: Gada System (Oromo):
• Indigenous democratic socio-political system
• Age-grade classes and leadership rotation
• Registered by UNESCO as World Heritage
Luwa System (Sidama):
• Mentoring, training, and initiation system for youth
• Generational class or age-set system
• Administered by democratic rules and principles
• Leader called gadana, deputy called jalawa
• Five cycles: Fulasa, Darara, Mogisa, Wawasa, Hirbora
• Each cycle rotates approximately every eight years
Dagu System (Afar):
• Indigenous information exchange system
• Called the 'Internet of the Afar'
• Every Afar plays role of a journalist, elders as editors
• 'Wireless network' for sharing factual information

slides.title: UNESCO Registered Heritages of Ethiopia
content: Cultural Heritage Sites:
• Tiya Stone Erections - UNESCO (1980)
- 46 large, decorated megaliths
- Cemetery site, dating between 10-15 centuries
• Harar Jugol, the Fortified Historic Town - UNESCO (2006)
- 'Fourth city of Islam' - 82 mosques, 102 shrines
- Five traditional gates (Asadin, Asum, Argob, Bedro, Sufat)
- Hyena men tradition
• Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela - UNESCO (1978)
• Castles of Gondar - UNESCO (1979)
• Obelisks of Aksum
• Konso Cultural Landscape - UNESCO (2011)
- 55 sq km arid property of stone-walled terraces
Intangible Cultural Heritage:
• Meskel Festival - UNESCO (2019)
• Fiche Chambalalla - UNESCO (2019)
• Gada System - UNESCO
Natural Heritage Site:
• Simen Mountains National Park - UNESCO (1978)
- 220 sq km, famous for scenery, Gelada Baboon, Walia Ibex
Not Yet Registered: Bale Mountains National Park
